summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Triable issues existed on the parents' procedural due process claim and the child's Fourth Amendment unreasonable-seizure claim arising from her removal from school without a court order, although the defendants retained qualified immunity because the rule was not clearly established in 1990.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the mere possibility of danger is not enough: emergency circumstances mean the child is immediately threatened with harm and there is no time to get an order.
key_cases.quote: where there is reasonable time consistent with the safety of the child to obtain a judicial order, the “emergency” removal of a child is unwarranted

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Agency lawyers who initiate and prosecute child-protective proceedings have absolute immunity from § 1983 claims, but caseworkers do not, because their removal decisions are the functional equivalent of an arrest; on these facts the caseworkers were nevertheless protected by qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: The decision fixes the immunity framework applicable to the emergency-removal decision itself in the Second Circuit, which includes Vermont.
key_cases.quote: The caseworker defendants are not entitled to absolute immunity on plaintiffs § 1983 claims because their actions were the functional equivalent of arresting officers in criminal cases.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the defendants was affirmed because during the relevant period the newborn was held by the hospital for medical reasons rather than by the child-welfare agency, so no Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment violation arose from the retention.
key_cases.relevance: The case marks the point at which continued retention becomes an agency removal decision requiring constitutional justification.
key_cases.quote: Mora was held by the Hospital for medical reasons, not concerns about possible parental mistreatment and CWA policies

key_cases.holding: A post-disposition order transferring custody of a child back to DCF is a final appealable order, and the preponderance standard, not clear and convincing evidence, governs it because the deprivation is temporary rather than a permanent severance.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that an emergency care order and later temporary transfers rest on a preponderance standard in Vermont.
key_cases.quote: In its decision to modify the plan to transfer legal custody of I.B. back to DCF, therefore, the trial court here applied the proper standard of proof.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; the Court held that suspension of parent-child contact under 33 V.S.A. § 5319(a) is a temporary deprivation that may be sustained on a preponderance showing that the suspension is necessary to protect the child's physical safety or emotional well-being, so no clear-and-convincing finding of unfitness was required at that stage.
key_cases.relevance: B.C. is the primary Vermont authority for the rule that state action working only a temporary deprivation of parental rights, including emergency and interim custody orders, is governed by the preponderance standard; In re I.B. quotes this case for that proposition.
key_cases.quote: state intervention which effects only a temporary deprivation of parental rights requires a lesser showing of proof by a preponderance of the evidence

key_cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the caseworker was vacated on the Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claims arising from a family-court entry order obtained through allegedly false statements, on the procedural due process claims, and on the children's Fourth Amendment unlawful-seizure claim, because qualified immunity could not be resolved as a matter of law on that record; summary judgment was affirmed only on the father's substantive due process claim.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a caseworker who procures the warrant-equivalent family-court entry order through knowingly false or misleading statements loses the presumption of reasonableness that order would supply, so the entry and removal are judged on a corrected record.
key_cases.quote: the Children's right not to be taken from the care of their parent without court order, parental consent, or emergency circumstances was firmly established

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to document the safety determination and safety plan on the SDM Safety Assessment
timeline_requirements.starts_from: First in-person interview with the family
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days to conclude an investigation; 45 days to complete an assessment, or 60 days with written justification and supervisor approval
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Opening of the child safety intervention (the investigation or assessment track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024); the policy allows an investigation to stay open past 60 days while a law enforcement or criminal case is unresolved, and an assessment extension may not exceed 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)). Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track by statute (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
